title: Ancient Egypt (Old, Middle, New Kingdoms)
titleline: Ancient Egypt (Old, Middle, New Kingdoms) - The History Web
para1: Ancient Egypt (Old, Middle, New Kingdoms). Ancient Egypt was one of the most enduring and iconic civilizations in human history, flourishing along the fertile banks of the Nile River from around 3100 BCE to 1070 BCE. Divided into three major golden ages, this monumental civilization matters deeply for its groundbreaking developments in architecture, mathematics, medicine, and writing systems like hieroglyphics. They established centralized rule under divine pharaohs and created a rich religious system centered on the afterlife, leaving behind timeless monuments like the Pyramids of Giza.
para2: Each of the three distinct eras expanded Egyptian power and artistic mastery, with the New Kingdom reaching an imperial peak that stretched deep into the Levant and Nubia. However, centuries of massive military campaigns, civil fragmentation, and severe economic strain eventually drained the state's central authority. Outside powers like the Libyans and Sea Peoples began launching constant invasions during the Bronze Age collapse. By the end of the New Kingdom, Egypt fractured into competing local dynasties, forever losing its absolute hegemony over the region.
para3: Economic life rested on the Nile and on grain. Farmers grew wheat and barley on the floodplain, paid taxes in kind to state and temple granaries, and owed labor on canals and monuments in the flood season when the fields lay under water. Around this agricultural core worked craftsmen, potters, weavers, carpenters, metalworkers, organized in palace and temple workshops, while expeditions brought gold from Nubia, copper and turquoise from Sinai, cedar from Lebanon, and incense from Punt, making Egypt rich enough to trade grain and linen across the eastern Mediterranean.
para4: Social life was layered but not frozen. Below the king came the officials, priests, and scribes; literacy was the great ladder, and a capable boy from a modest family could rise through the scribal schools. Most Egyptians were peasant families working small plots, yet their world was not joyless: beer and bread at every meal, festivals at the local temple, board games like senet, music and wrestling, and legal rights for women, who could own property, bring cases to court, and inherit, that were unusual in the ancient world. We know their daily lives unusually well from the workmen's village of Deir el-Medina, whose records include laundry lists, love songs, lawsuits, and what may be history's first recorded sit-down strike.
para5: Religion gave this society its framework of meaning. The king was responsible for ma'at, the order of the world, and the great temples, above all Amun's at Karnak, stood at the center of the country's economic as well as religious life; their festivals, like the Opet procession from Karnak to Luxor, were the public holidays of the year. Belief in the afterlife shaped Egyptian civilization from the pyramids to the painted tombs, and over time its hope widened from a royal privilege to a promise for ordinary people, a change visible in the spread of funerary texts and Osiris worship in the Middle and New Kingdoms.
para6: Cultural life was anchored in writing and its institutions. Hieroglyphs carved the record in stone while scribes wrote the same language in cursive on papyrus; scribal schools trained the administrators who ran everything. Egyptians produced wisdom instructions, tales such as Sinuhe, hymns and love poetry, and practical science in the service of real problems: a 365-day calendar tied to the flood and the star Sirius, mathematics for surveying and building, and medicine recorded in case-by-case papyri whose clinical observations still impress modern readers. Measured across its three kingdoms, Egypt's deepest achievement was this complete, durable pattern of economic, social, religious, and cultural life, one that neighboring peoples borrowed from and later ages kept rediscovering.

title: Carthage
titleline: Carthage - The History Web
para1: Carthage was a powerful ancient thalassocracy based in modern day Tunisia, founded as a Phoenician trading colony in 814 BCE. Occupying an exceptionally strategic position in the central Mediterranean, it transformed into an economic and military powerhouse that built a sprawling trade empire. Carthage is historically critical because it long dominated the maritime commerce of the western Mediterranean, establishing colonies across North Africa, Spain, and Sicily. They commanded legendary naval fleets and controlled the flow of precious metals, agricultural goods, and luxury items throughout the western world.
para2: Carthage was governed not by kings but by elected magistrates called suffetes, advised by a senate of leading families and watched by a powerful court of a hundred and four judges; Aristotle, who knew the city by reputation, counted its constitution among the best designed of the ancient world. Its people lived in a crowded merchant metropolis of tall houses, workshops, and temples around the Byrsa hill, and its double harbor, one basin for traders and one for warships, held hundreds of docks where the fleets that ruled the western seas were built, supplied, and repaired.
para3: This dominance brought them into a series of catastrophic conflicts with the expanding Roman Republic, known as the Punic Wars. Despite the genius of Hannibal Barca, who famously marched elephants over the Alps to inflict crushing defeats on Roman legions, Carthage could not match Rome's relentless manpower. The Third Punic War ended in 146 BCE with the total destruction of Carthage by Roman forces. The city was completely burned, its surviving citizens were sold into slavery, and its vast territories were absorbed into the Roman Empire.
para4: The empire's wealth had come from farms as much as ships: Carthaginian writers like Mago produced the most respected agricultural manuals of their time, and the fields of North Africa fed the city and supplied its exports. Greek and Roman writers report that the Carthaginians sacrificed children to the gods Baal Hammon and Tanit in a precinct called the tophet; how literally to read those enemy accounts is still debated by archaeologists. Rome refounded the city about a century after the destruction, it grew again into one of the greatest cities of the Roman Empire, and the Punic language lingered in the African countryside for centuries.

title: Mauretania
titleline: Mauretania - The History Web
para1: Mauretania was an ancient Berber kingdom situated on the Atlantic coast of North Africa, encompassing modern day Morocco and western Algeria from the 3rd century BCE to 40 CE. Inhabited by the Mauri people, this tribal kingdom matters because it controlled crucial Atlantic and Mediterranean trade networks, supplying the ancient world with fine horses, timber, and valuable purple dyes. For much of its early history, Mauretania maintained a strong, independent identity while skillfully navigating the intense geopolitical rivalries between Carthage and Rome.
para2: The kingdom's wealth rested on its land and coasts: Mauretania produced grain, olives, marble, timber, and livestock, and its shores were famous for Tyrian purple, the snail-based dye prized across the ancient world. As Carthage's power faded after its defeats by Rome, Mauretanian kings took over old Phoenician ports like Tingis, and later rulers even minted their own coins, some lettered in Phoenician and some in Latin, a sign of a kingdom balanced between worlds. Its kings played the great powers with care: Bocchus I first allied with, and then betrayed, his son-in-law Jugurtha of Numidia to the Romans, and his successors backed Julius Caesar in the civil wars, earning Roman favor and territory.
para3: The kingdom eventually entered the Roman political orbit as a loyal client state, reaching its cultural and economic peak under King Juba II, appointed by Augustus, and his wife Cleopatra Selene II, a daughter of Cleopatra of Egypt. Raised in Rome, Juba pushed his still mostly pastoral people toward city life, expanding the cities of Volubilis and Caesarea with Greco-Roman temples, palaces, and theaters, though the great royal mausoleum built in his reign followed older Berber forms. As Roman clients, his dynasty faced repeated revolts in the mountain interior and raids from the desert tribes, and Rome repeatedly had to send help.
para4: This prosperous era came to an abrupt end in 40 CE, when the Roman Emperor Caligula had Mauretania's final king, Ptolemy, executed over a perceived slight. A major anti-Roman rebellion erupted shortly after, and after crushing it Rome formally divided the kingdom in 44 CE into two imperial provinces, ending the old Berber monarchy for good.

title: Numidia
titleline: Numidia - The History Web
para1: Numidia was an ancient Berber kingdom located in modern day Algeria and parts of Tunisia, flourishing from the 3rd century BCE until its annexation by Rome in 46 BCE. Originally composed of two semi-nomadic confederations, the kingdom was unified under King Masinissa following his strategic alliance with Rome during the Second Punic War.
para2: The Numidians entered world history on horseback: divided between the Massylii of the east and the Masaesyli of the west, their matchless light cavalry fought first for Carthage and then, when the young prince Masinissa changed sides, for Rome. It was Masinissa's horsemen who helped the Roman general Scipio break Hannibal's army at Zama in 202 BCE, and a united Numidian kingdom under Roman favor was his reward.
para3: Numidia is historically important because it proved to be an indispensable regional player in the western Mediterranean. Their legendary light cavalry was widely considered the finest in the ancient world, playing a decisive role in major battles across Europe and North Africa. Under Masinissa's long reign of more than half a century, Numidia rapidly transformed from a loose pastoral society into a settled, urbanized agricultural power whose grain surpluses were exported across the Mediterranean.
para4: However, later dynastic struggles invited aggressive political and military interference from the Roman Senate. The famous Jugurthine War showcased widespread Roman corruption and deep Numidian tactical skill before King Jugurtha was betrayed by his own ally, the Mauretanian king Bocchus, captured, and executed in Rome. The kingdom was permanently broken up into smaller client states and eventually absorbed as a Roman province by Julius Caesar.
para5: The end came through Rome's own civil wars: King Juba I of Numidia backed Pompey against Julius Caesar, and after Caesar crushed him at the battle of Thapsus in 46 BCE, the kingdom was annexed outright. Under Roman rule its old royal city of Cirta, rebuilt as Constantine, and the legionary base at Lambaesis became centers of a prosperous African province whose farmland helped feed Rome, a second life on the ruins of the first.

title: Ptolemaic Egypt
titleline: Ptolemaic Egypt - The History Web
para1: Ptolemaic Egypt was a powerful Hellenistic kingdom that ruled the Nile valley from 305 BCE to 30 BCE following the death of Alexander the Great. Founded by Alexander's Macedonian general Ptolemy I, the dynasty established its spectacular capital at Alexandria on the Mediterranean coast. This kingdom is historically vital because it created a brilliant synthesis of Greek and ancient Egyptian cultures, turning Alexandria into the leading intellectual center of the Mediterranean world. They constructed the iconic Great Library and the Lighthouse of Alexandria, attracting master scholars from across the Mediterranean.
para2: The dynasty's founder set the tone with a single bold stroke: Ptolemy I intercepted the mummified body of Alexander the Great on its journey back to Macedonia and buried it in Alexandria, binding his new kingdom to the conqueror's glory. Greek settlers ran the administration from above while Egyptian priests kept their temples and traditions, and the court promoted a new shared god, Serapis, who blended Greek and Egyptian forms for both peoples. Even the era's most famous stone tells this double story: the Rosetta Stone, a priestly decree of 196 BCE carved in Greek and Egyptian scripts, would one day give modern scholars the key to the hieroglyphs.
para3: Alexandria's Library and Museum made the city the workshop of ancient science: there Euclid systematized geometry, Eratosthenes measured the circumference of the earth with remarkable accuracy, and physicians made pioneering studies of the human body. The kingdom's wealth flowed from the Nile, through royal monopolies on oil, banking, and textiles and grain fleets that fed cities across the Mediterranean.
para4: While the ruling elite remained strictly Greek speaking, they adopted traditional Egyptian royal titles and heavily patronized local temples to maintain internal order. Over time, severe dynastic infighting and frequent native rebellions deeply weakened the kingdom's political foundation. The realm became increasingly dependent on the rising military power of the Roman Republic to protect its borders. The dynasty finally met its end when Queen Cleopatra VII and Mark Antony were defeated by Octavian, leading to Egypt's direct annexation as a wealthy Roman province.

title: Roman North Africa
titleline: Roman North Africa - The History Web
para1: Roman North Africa refers to the vast, wealthy coastal territories of the Mediterranean margin including modern Tunisia, Algeria, Libya, and Morocco under Roman rule from 146 BCE through late antiquity. Known widely as the granary of Rome, this region was vital to the empire because its massive grain yields and olive oil production literally fed the imperial capital. It became one of the most heavily urbanized and prosperous zones of the Roman world, producing breathtaking stone cities like Timgad and Leptis Magna featuring incredible aqueducts, theaters, and mosaics.
para2: The engine of this prosperity was the farm and the workshop. The province of Africa had a specific task in the imperial system: it had to provide Rome with grain, and fleet after fleet loaded with wheat, olive oil, and garum, the prized fish sauce of the Roman table, sailed from African harbors. African red slip pottery became one of the most widely distributed wares in the entire empire, found by archaeologists in most of its major cities, and the region suffered so little during the crises of the third century that its exports only grew.
para3: Its stone cities still stun visitors: Timgad, founded for the emperor Trajan's veterans and laid out with the regularity of a military camp; Leptis Magna, the hometown of the emperor Septimius Severus; and Carthage itself, rebuilt by Rome into one of the five largest cities of the Mediterranean world. The region was also a furnace of early Christianity: it produced the theologian Tertullian, endured the long Donatist schism that split African churches, and gave the world Augustine of Hippo, whose writings shaped Western thought.
para4: Beyond its immense economic weight, the region played a pivotal role in the intellectual and religious evolution of the Roman Empire. The long period of Roman stability was eventually shattered in the 5th century CE when the Vandals crossed the Strait of Gibraltar and conquered the major coastal cities. While the Byzantines briefly reclaimed parts of the region in the 6th century, Roman North Africa was permanently transformed in the 7th century by the sweeping Arab Islamic conquests, which took Carthage in 698 and folded the old Roman coast into a new world.
source4label: World History Encyclopedia: The Splendours of Roman Algeria

title: The Kingdom of Aksum
titleline: The Kingdom of Aksum - The History Web
para1: The Kingdom of Aksum was a major trading empire centered in modern day northern Ethiopia and Eritrea that flourished from the 1st to the 8th centuries CE. Perfectly positioned along crucial Red Sea maritime routes, it connected the Roman Empire to India, and a 3rd century Persian writer counted Aksum among the four great powers of the world, alongside Rome, Persia, and China. This state matters immensely because it adopted Christianity as its official religion in the 4th century CE under King Ezana, establishing one of the oldest national churches in human history and issuing its own unique gold coinage.
para2: Its wealth flowed through the port of Adulis, where camel caravans carried gold, ivory, incense, and other treasures of the African interior to exchange for textiles, weapons, and glassware from India and the Roman world, and Aksumite coins have turned up as far away as India and Sri Lanka. Aksum was the first sub Saharan African state to mint its own coinage, and it developed its own script, Ge'ez, which still serves as the liturgical language of the Ethiopian Church today.
para3: Its stone engineering remains breathtaking: the royal cemetery holds towering granite stelae carved to resemble multi story palaces, and one fallen example measures 33 meters and 520 tonnes, the largest single stone ever transported anywhere in antiquity. Aksum reached its absolute zenith by projecting power across the Red Sea to rule parts of the Arabian Peninsula, most notably under King Kaleb in the 6th century, whose armies, backed by long standing ties to Byzantium, governed Yemen until the Sasanian Persians arrived in 570.
para4: In the mid 4th century, Ezana's armies had also sacked Meroe, capital of the fading kingdom of Kush, clearing Aksum's path to dominate the region. However, the kingdom began a slow decline in the 7th century as the newly emerging Islamic caliphates gained control of Red Sea trade routes, effectively isolating Aksum economically. Environmental degradation and climate shifts further eroded their agricultural output. The capital was eventually abandoned, and the political center shifted south into the Ethiopian highlands, setting the stage for the medieval Zagwe dynasty.
source2label: World History Encyclopedia: Kingdom of Axum
source3label: Humanities LibreTexts: 11.1: Kingdom of Aksum

title: The Kingdom of Kush / Nubia
titleline: The Kingdom of Kush / Nubia - The History Web
para1: The Kingdom of Kush was an ancient African empire centered along the Middle Nile in modern day Sudan, flourishing from roughly 1000 BCE to 350 CE. Operating directly south of Egypt, it grew wealthy through its vast iron deposits, gold mines, and control over lucrative trade routes connecting sub Saharan Africa to the Mediterranean. Kush matters greatly to world history because it proved that complex, highly urbanized centers could thrive in the upper Nile region on their own terms, absorbing Egyptian influences yet never merely copying them. They developed their own unique Meroitic script and built hundreds of distinct, steep sided pyramids, more of them than survive in Egypt itself.
para2: Its heartland was rich in the goods the ancient world craved: gold from the desert mines, ivory and ebony from the south, and cattle in great herds. In its later centuries, the iron furnaces of Meroe left slag heaps so massive that they still rise around the city's ruins today, earning Kush a reputation as a center of ancient African industry.
para3: Kushite culture blended Egyptian forms with a style all its own. Kushite kings sometimes ruled through their queens: the kandakes, or queen mothers, held real power, and one of them, Amanirenas, fought the armies of the Roman emperor Augustus to a negotiated peace on favorable terms. The kingdom devised the Meroitic script, whose letters can now be read but whose language remains largely untranslated.
para4: The Kushites achieved their absolute political peak during the 8th century BCE, when King Piye led a massive army north to conquer Egypt and establish the Twenty Fifth Dynasty. They ruled both lands as legitimate pharaohs for nearly a century before being driven back south by invading Assyrian armies. Re-establishing their capital at Meroe, the kingdom maintained its economic prosperity and architectural splendor for centuries. The state eventually faded in the 4th century CE, weakened by environmental degradation, and the final blow came from the south, where Aksumite armies sacked Meroe and took over the region's trade.
source2label: World History Encyclopedia: The Kingdom of Kush
source3label: Humanities LibreTexts: 7.8: Ancient Nubia and the Kingdom of Kush

title: The Land of Punt
titleline: The Land of Punt - The History Web
para1: The Land of Punt was an ancient, highly prosperous trading kingdom located somewhere along the Horn of Africa, flourishing from roughly 2500 BCE to 1000 BCE. Revered by ancient Egyptians as God's Land, Punt matters greatly to history because it served as a major regional commercial hub connecting interior Africa to the Red Sea. Trade was ancient long before it was famous: Egyptian records hint at voyages to Punt as early as the reign of Khufu in the 26th century BCE. They produced highly sought after luxury goods, most notably frankincense, myrrh, gold, ebony, ivory, and wild exotic animals that were eagerly imported by Egyptian pharaohs for religious rituals.
para2: The most famous record of this kingdom comes from the temple walls of Queen Hatshepsut at Deir el-Bahari, which vividly depict a massive Egyptian naval expedition trading peacefully with Punt's king and queen. The fleet returned loaded with treasures, including living incense trees transplanted to Egyptian soil, the first known successful transplanting of foreign flora in recorded history. These detailed reliefs showcase stilt houses, lush palm trees, and dense marine life, offering invaluable glimpses into ancient East African society.
para3: The kingdom slowly faded from Egyptian records during the Late Bronze Age collapse as trade routes deteriorated, with the last great recorded expeditions under the New Kingdom's final warrior pharaohs. While Punt's exact geographical boundaries remain debated by modern historians, with scholars proposing Somalia, Eritrea, Sudan, or even Arabia, the Red Sea lanes it anchored would one day carry the rise of Aksum.
para4: The search for Punt is a detective story of its own. The Egyptians called it Pwenet, a name later Greek geographers echoed as Opone, and the debate over its location began soon after Champollion first deciphered hieroglyphs in 1822. Eritrea and northwest Somalia remain the leading candidates today, and observers note striking resemblances between the region's traditional dress, arts, and the figures carved on Hatshepsut's walls, hints of a very ancient exchange between Egypt and the Horn.
source2label: World History Encyclopedia: Supposed Location of the Land of Punt
source3label: Humanities LibreTexts: 4.4: Ancient Egyptian Trade

title: The Nok Culture
titleline: The Nok Culture - The History Web
para1: The Nok Culture was an advanced Iron Age society that flourished on the Jos Plateau in modern central Nigeria during the second and first millennia BCE. Long-running archaeological fieldwork dates the culture's emergence to about 1500 BCE and its fading to around the turn of the era, while its famous terracotta art belongs mainly to the centuries after 900 BCE, dated by the Metropolitan Museum to about 500 BCE-200 CE. They matter immensely to African history because they were among the earliest known societies in West Africa to master iron smelting, jumping straight from the Stone Age to the Iron Age without the long bronze working stage seen elsewhere. Whether that knowledge arrived from Carthage, from Nubia, or was a purely local invention remains one of African archaeology's open questions. Iron agricultural tools and hunting weapons drove population growth and complex social structures across the region long before extensive outside contact.
para2: At Taruga, the oldest known Nok settlement, archaeologists uncovered the remains of no fewer than thirteen iron smelting furnaces. Iron hoes, axes, and cleavers boosted farm output, letting Nok farmers raise sorghum and vegetables across a territory that may have covered 78,000 square kilometers, about the size of Portugal, though stone tools never disappeared, a sign that metal stayed precious.
para3: The culture is world famous today for its extraordinary, highly distinctive terracotta sculptures, featuring intricate hairstyles, detailed jewelry, and stylized expressive faces, the earliest known art of its kind in West Africa. The first of them surfaced by accident in the 20th century, tossed up by tin mining near the village of Nok that gave the culture its modern name. These artistic masterpieces suggest a sophisticated religious or funerary tradition, though their exact cultural meaning remains uncertain due to a lack of written records.
para4: The culture faded around the turn of the era: its characteristic pottery drops sharply from the archaeological record, and climate shifts, deforestation from iron smelting, or pressure from rival peoples may all have played a part. Despite their physical disappearance, their artistic and metallurgical traditions deeply influenced later West African civilizations like the Kingdom of Ife.
source2label: World History Encyclopedia: Nok Culture
source3label: Humanities LibreTexts: 9.1: Nok Culture of Ancient Africa

title: Pre-dynastic Egypt and the Unification
titleline: Pre-dynastic Egypt and the Unification - The History Web
para1: Pre-dynastic Egypt and the Unification. The Predynastic period of ancient Egypt (c. 6000-3100 BC) covers the long centuries in which farming communities along the Nile grew into one of the first territorial states in world history. After the end of the last Ice Age, communities such as the Badarian culture in Upper Egypt began cultivating wheat and barley, herding cattle, and making pottery by about 5000 BC. They were followed by the Naqada culture, which expanded gradually from its heartland around the city of Naqada and developed increasingly sophisticated crafts, long-distance trade, and social ranking.
para2: During the Naqada II and III phases (c. 3500-3100 BC), Upper Egyptian centers such as Hierakonpolis and Abydos became seats of powerful local rulers. Cemeteries show clear differences in wealth, and craftsmen produced fine pottery, stone vessels, and ceremonial palettes carved with images of kingship, war, and animals. Trade brought gold from Nubia, lapis lazuli from distant Afghanistan, and timber and pottery contacts with Mesopotamia and the Levant, and by the end of the period the earliest Egyptian hieroglyphic writing appeared on labels and monuments.
para3: The unification of Egypt was the work of a series of Upper Egyptian kings, known from names such as Iry-Hor, Ka, and Scorpion, who brought the Delta under their control in the late fourth millennium. The process culminated around 3100 BC with King Narmer, whose ceremonial palette shows him wearing the crowns of both Upper and Lower Egypt and smiting his enemies. Later tradition remembered the unifier as Menes, founder of the First Dynasty and of the new capital at Memphis, near the meeting point of the valley and the Delta.
para4: The significance of this period can hardly be overstated. The unification created a single kingdom stretching from the Mediterranean to the First Cataract, governed from one center and held together by writing, taxation, and royal ritual. The institutions, artistic conventions, and religious ideas worked out in these centuries became the foundation of pharaonic civilization, which endured for three thousand years and remains one of the most remarkable achievements of the ancient world.
source1label: World History Encyclopedia: Predynastic Period in Egypt
source2label: Britannica: Menes
source3label: Britannica: Ancient Egypt

title: Akhenaten and the Amarna Period
titleline: Akhenaten and the Amarna Period - The History Web
para1: Akhenaten and the Amarna Period. The Amarna Period (c. 1353-1336 BC) was the brief and astonishing chapter of the Eighteenth Dynasty in which Pharaoh Amenhotep IV, who took the name Akhenaten, tried to remake Egyptian religion and art around a single god. In the early years of his reign he promoted the Aten, the visible disk of the sun, above the traditional gods, and in his fifth year he founded an entirely new capital, Akhetaten, known today as Amarna, on a virgin site in Middle Egypt.
para2: Akhenaten's religious program grew steadily more radical. The Aten was worshipped in open-air temples filled with sunlight, praised in the Great Hymn to the Aten as the sole creator who sustains all lands. In the later part of the reign the king ordered the names of Amun and other gods chiseled out of monuments, closing their temples and redirecting their vast revenues to the Aten. Art changed just as dramatically: the so-called Amarna style showed the royal family with elongated faces, heavy hips, and intimate domestic scenes beneath the rays of the Aten, a striking break from the rigid conventions of earlier Egyptian art.
para3: The period is unusually well documented because of the Amarna Letters, a cache of nearly four hundred clay tablets found at the site. These diplomatic letters, written in Akkadian, record exchanges between the Egyptian court and the kings of Babylon, Assyria, Mitanni, and the Hittites, as well as desperate appeals from Canaanite vassal rulers begging for troops. Scholars long blamed Akhenaten for neglecting the empire while rivals such as the Hittite king Suppiluliuma expanded, though modern research suggests the crown remained more active abroad than was once thought.
para4: The revolution did not survive its founder. Akhenaten died around 1336 BC, and after the brief reigns of Smenkhkare and Neferneferuaten, the boy king Tutankhamun restored the old gods and abandoned Amarna. Under Horemheb and the early Nineteenth Dynasty, Akhenaten's monuments were torn down and his name erased from king lists. Yet the Amarna Period remains one of the most debated episodes in Egyptian history, studied as a unique experiment in monotheistic worship, royal propaganda, and artistic freedom.
source2label: World History Encyclopedia: Amarna Period of Egypt
source3label: Metropolitan Museum of Art: Art and City under Akhenaten
source4label: UCL Digital Egypt: The Amarna Period

title: Ramesses II and the Late Bronze Age Collapse
titleline: Ramesses II and the Late Bronze Age Collapse - The History Web
para1: Ramesses II and the Late Bronze Age Collapse. Ramesses II (reigned 1279-1213 BC), third king of the Nineteenth Dynasty, ruled Egypt for sixty-six years and became the very model of a pharaoh. He built on a scale few rulers have ever matched: a new capital at Pi-Ramesses in the Delta, the mortuary temple known as the Ramesseum at Thebes, the rock-cut temples of Abu Simbel in Nubia, and additions at Karnak and Luxor, covering Egypt with colossal statues of himself.
para2: Early in his reign Ramesses marched into Syria to contest the Hittite Empire, and around 1274 BC he fought the Battle of Kadesh against King Muwatalli II. Ramesses was nearly trapped when Hittite chariots ambushed his marching columns, but he rallied his forces and held the field. He proclaimed the battle a great victory on temple walls across Egypt, yet the strategic situation barely changed, and years later Egypt and the Hittites concluded a formal peace treaty under Hattusili III. A copy of that treaty survives and is often called the earliest international peace agreement in history.
para3: Ramesses outlived most of his many sons and was succeeded by his thirteenth son, Merneptah, under whom Egypt defeated an invasion of Libyans allied with groups of the Sea Peoples. His grandson in turn, Ramesses III of the Twentieth Dynasty, fought the Sea Peoples again around 1178 BC, destroying their ships and armies in battles depicted at Medinet Habu. Egypt survived these invasions, but the strain was enormous and the empire in Asia gradually slipped away.
para4: These wars belonged to a wider catastrophe known as the Late Bronze Age Collapse (c. 1200-1150 BC). Within a few generations the Hittite Empire vanished, the city of Ugarit was burned, the Mycenaean palaces of Greece were destroyed, and trade networks across the eastern Mediterranean broke down. Scholars debate the causes, pointing to migrating peoples, drought and famine, earthquakes, and the fragility of palace economies. Egypt endured as a state, but the world of Bronze Age great powers was gone, and the Iron Age that followed belonged to new peoples.
source2label: World History Encyclopedia: Bronze Age Collapse
source3label: World History Encyclopedia: Sea Peoples
source4label: Princeton University Press: 1177 B.C.: The Year Civilization Collapsed

title: The Third Intermediate Period and the Libyan Dynasties
titleline: The Third Intermediate Period and the Libyan Dynasties - The History Web
para1: The Third Intermediate Period and the Libyan Dynasties. The Third Intermediate Period (c. 1069-664 BC) followed the death of Ramesses XI and the end of the New Kingdom, and it was defined above all by division. Smendes founded the Twenty-first Dynasty ruling from Tanis in the Delta, while in the south the High Priests of Amun at Thebes, beginning with Herihor and Pinedjem, governed Upper Egypt as a semi-independent theocracy that nominally recognized the northern kings.
para2: From about 945 BC Egypt came under the rule of Libyan dynasties, descended from Meshwesh and Libu warriors who had settled in Egypt over generations. Shoshenq I, founder of the Twenty-second Dynasty at Bubastis, reunited the country and in 925 BC campaigned in Palestine, appearing in the Hebrew Bible as Shishak, the king who plundered the treasures of Jerusalem. His successors, including Osorkon I and Osorkon II, presided over a stable kingdom, but authority gradually splintered as local Libyan chiefs and a rival Twenty-third Dynasty claimed royal titles in different cities.
para3: In the western Delta, Tefnakht of Sais built the Twenty-fourth Dynasty and pushed south, but his expansion provoked the rising Kingdom of Kush to the south. The Kushite king Piye marched north around 728 BC and recorded his conquest of all Egypt on a great victory stela. His brother Shabaqa then established the Twenty-fifth Dynasty, and for nearly a century Kushite pharaohs such as Taharqa ruled both Nubia and Egypt, reviving pyramid building and supporting the temples.
para4: Kushite rule collided with the expanding Assyrian Empire. Assyrian armies under Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal invaded Egypt, drove out Taharqa and his successor Tanutamani, and sacked Thebes in 663 BC, carrying off enormous booty. The Assyrians withdrew, leaving their client Psamtik of Sais to found the Twenty-sixth Dynasty. The Third Intermediate Period thus forms a bridge between the New Kingdom and the Late Period: an age of political fragmentation, foreign dynasties, and shifting capitals, during which Egyptian religion, art, and temple life nonetheless remained remarkably alive.

title: The Saite Dynasty and the Late Period
titleline: The Saite Dynasty and the Late Period - The History Web
para1: The Saite Dynasty and the Late Period. The Late Period of ancient Egypt (664-332 BC) began when Psamtik I, ruler of Sais in the western Delta, shook off Assyrian control and reunited the country, founding the Twenty-sixth Dynasty. With the help of Greek and Carian mercenaries he secured his throne, opened Egypt to foreign merchants, and presided over a deliberate revival of the art, texts, and monuments of Egypt's Old and Middle Kingdom past, an archaizing style that gave the age its distinctive polished look.
para2: The Saite century was prosperous and outward-looking. Necho II began a canal linking the Nile to the Red Sea, an ancestor of the Suez Canal, and according to Herodotus he sent Phoenician sailors on a voyage that circled the whole of Africa. The Greek trading city of Naukratis flourished in the Delta, connecting Egypt to the Mediterranean world. Militarily the dynasty was less fortunate: Necho's victory over Judah at Megiddo was followed by a crushing defeat at the hands of the Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar at Carchemish in 605 BC, ending Egyptian ambitions in Asia.
para3: In 525 BC the Persian king Cambyses invaded, defeated Pharaoh Psamtik III at Pelusium, and made Egypt a province of the Persian Empire, the Twenty-seventh Dynasty. Persian rule was resented and repeatedly shaken off: Egyptians under Amyrtaeus, then the native Twenty-ninth and Thirtieth Dynasties of Nepherites, Nectanebo I, and Nectanebo II, ruled independently for some sixty years, rebuilding temples and defending the country until the Persians returned in 343 BC. Nectanebo II, who fled to Nubia, was the last native pharaoh of Egypt.
para4: The second Persian period was short. In 332 BC Alexander of Macedon entered Egypt without a fight, was welcomed as a liberator, and founded Alexandria before marching east. After his death his general Ptolemy took Egypt and began three centuries of Greek rule. The Late Period is remembered as the final flowering of native Egyptian statehood: an age when Egypt was wealthy, militarily active, and deeply conscious of its own ancient past, even as foreign empires closed in from every side.

title: Roman Egypt
titleline: Roman Egypt - The History Web
para1: Roman Egypt. Roman Egypt began in 30 BC, when Octavian, soon to be the emperor Augustus, annexed the kingdom after the defeat and death of Cleopatra VII and Mark Antony. Because Egypt produced much of the grain that fed Rome, the emperors treated it as a special possession: it was governed not by a senator but by a prefect appointed directly by the emperor, and Roman senators were forbidden even to visit without permission. Alexandria remained one of the greatest cities of the Mediterranean world, a center of commerce and learning.
para2: Life under Rome mixed old and new. Egyptian temples were still built and decorated in pharaonic style, as at Dendera, Edfu, and Philae, while the population paid heavy taxes and supplied grain fleets to Italy. In the Fayum depression, land reclamation created prosperous farming towns whose dead were buried with the famous Fayum mummy portraits, realistic painted faces on wooden panels that blend Egyptian burial customs with Greco-Roman art. Greek papyri preserved in the dry sands give an unmatched picture of everyday life, from tax receipts to private letters.
para3: From the first centuries AD, Christianity spread through Egypt and transformed it. Alexandria became a leading center of Christian scholarship, home to Origen and later to the great patriarch Athanasius, whose defense of orthodox doctrine shaped the Council of Nicaea. In the deserts, hermits such as Anthony and communities organized by Pachomius invented Christian monasticism, which spread across the empire. The old temples slowly closed; the last known hieroglyphic inscription was carved at Philae in AD 394, and the temple of Isis there was finally shut in the sixth century.
para4: Roman, and later Byzantine, rule in Egypt lasted six and a half centuries. Persian armies occupied the country from 619 to 629, and in 641 the Arab army of Amr ibn al-As took Byzantine Egypt, ending the ancient provincial order for good. Roman Egypt matters to historians because of its extraordinary documentation, its role in feeding the empire, and its place in the rise of Christianity, and because the Coptic church that grew from it still links modern Egypt to this long chapter of its past.

title: The Garamantes
titleline: The Garamantes - The History Web
para1: The Garamantes. The Garamantes (c. 500 BC - AD 700) were the people of a remarkable kingdom in the Fezzan, the desert heart of modern Libya, who proved that a complex state could flourish in the middle of the Sahara. Greek writers knew them from the fifth century BC: Herodotus described them as a powerful people who hunted the cave-dwelling Ethiopians in chariots and spread soil over salt-encrusted ground to grow their crops. Their capital, Garama, stood near modern Germa in the Wadi al-Ajal.
para2: The secret of Garamantian power lay underground. From early in their history they dug foggaras, gently sloping tunnels that tapped fossil water in the rock and carried it, sometimes for kilometers, to fields of wheat, barley, grapes, and dates. Hundreds of these channels, with lines of vertical maintenance shafts still visible from the air, supported farming towns and a growing population in one of the driest regions on Earth. Archaeological work in the Fezzan has revealed mud-brick cities, fortified settlements, and vast cemeteries with tens of thousands of tombs.
para3: The Garamantes stood at the southern end of trans-Saharan routes, and their relations with Rome were sometimes peaceful and sometimes hostile. Roman forces campaigned against them, notably under Cornelius Balbus in 19 BC, yet trade mattered more than war: gold, ivory, enslaved people, salt, and the gemstones Romans called carbuncles moved north through Garamantian hands, while wine, oil, and Roman goods flowed south. Diplomatic missions traveled between the Garamantian kings and Roman North Africa, and Roman writers counted Garama among the notable cities subdued or visited by their armies.
para4: The kingdom endured for roughly a thousand years, a record few ancient states can match. Its decline came with the drying of the climate, the falling water table that made the foggaras ever harder to maintain, and shifts in trade routes, and by the early Islamic period Garama was a shadow of itself. Today the Garamantes are recognized as one of the earliest urban societies of the Sahara, a reminder that the desert was never an empty barrier but a region crossed, farmed, and ruled by Africans long before the age of the great camel caravans.

title: The Hyksos Period
titleline: The Hyksos Period - The History Web
para1: The Hyksos Period. The Hyksos Period (c. 1650-1550 BC), known to Egyptians as the era of the rulers of foreign lands, was the first time a foreign people ruled a large part of Egypt. During the late Middle Kingdom, communities of western Asiatic settlers had grown up in the eastern Nile Delta, and as central authority collapsed in the Thirteenth Dynasty, their leaders took power. The Hyksos ruled from Avaris, modern Tell el-Dab'a, as the Fifteenth Dynasty, controlling the Delta and much of Lower Egypt while native Egyptian dynasties held on in Thebes.
para2: The Hyksos were not simply destructive invaders. Archaeology at Avaris shows a flourishing city blending Egyptian and Levantine culture, and the Hyksos kings adopted pharaonic titles, administration, and scribal traditions. Their century of rule brought important innovations into wider Egyptian use, including the horse and chariot, new bronze-working techniques, improved weapons such as the composite bow, new crops and olive cultivation, and new musical instruments and styles of dress. Trade connected their kingdom with Cyprus, Crete, and the Levant.
para3: Native Egyptian power recovered in Thebes, where the Seventeenth Dynasty gradually turned from vassalage to resistance. King Seqenenre Tao apparently died fighting, his mummy bearing terrible head wounds, and his son Kamose campaigned north against King Apophis, boasting of the fight on surviving stelae. The final victory fell to Kamose's brother Ahmose I, who besieged and captured Avaris around 1550 BC, drove the Hyksos from Egypt, and pursued them into the southern Levant.
para4: The expulsion of the Hyksos founded the Eighteenth Dynasty and opened the New Kingdom, the age of Egypt's greatest empire. The experience of foreign rule had transformed Egypt: its rulers now built a standing army equipped with chariots, campaigned deep into Asia, and created an empire partly to ensure no foreign power could ever again dominate the Nile Valley. The Hyksos Period, once remembered with shame as a humiliation, thus became the catalyst for the most powerful era in pharaonic history.

title: The Blemmyes and the Nobades
titleline: The Blemmyes and the Nobades - The History Web
para1: The Blemmyes and the Nobades. The Blemmyes and the Nobades (c. AD 250-650) were the two peoples who dominated Lower Nubia between the fall of the Kushite kingdom of Meroe and the rise of the Christian Nubian kingdoms. When Meroe collapsed in the fourth century, its former northern lands fragmented, and into the vacuum moved the Nobades, a people settled along the Nile from the First to the Second Cataract, and the Blemmyes, desert nomads of the Eastern Desert between the Nile and the Red Sea.
para2: The Blemmyes were already old enemies of Rome. From the third century they raided the southern Egyptian frontier so persistently that the emperor Diocletian pulled the Roman border back to the First Cataract around AD 298 and paid both peoples subsidies to keep the peace. Blemmye war bands at times occupied the Dodekaschoinos, the stretch of river below the cataract, and the great temple complex of Philae passed back and forth between Roman and Blemmye control. Their chiefs ruled from the desert and from towns such as Talmis, and their power rested on camel-borne mobility across the eastern wastes.
para3: The Nobades, meanwhile, built a settled riverine kingdom with its centers at Faras and later Dongola. Their rulers buried their dead in great tumulus tombs at Ballana and Qustul, filled with weapons, horse gear, jewelry, and silver crowns that show both the wealth of the Nile trade and continuing contact with Egypt. Ancient writers describe repeated wars between the Nobades and the Blemmyes, until in the mid-fifth century the Nobadian king Silko recorded in an inscription at Kalabsha that he had defeated the Blemmyes and driven them from the Nile valley.
para4: These two peoples formed the bridge between the ancient and medieval worlds in Nubia. From the realm of the Nobades emerged the Christian kingdom of Nobatia, converted in the sixth century, while the Blemmyes lingered in the Eastern Desert for centuries more. Their era saw Nubia move from the orbit of pharaonic and Roman Egypt toward the Christian kingdoms of Makuria and Alodia, which would dominate the middle Nile for nearly a thousand years.

title: The Nubian Christian Kingdoms
titleline: The Nubian Christian Kingdoms - The History Web
para1: The Nubian Christian Kingdoms. The Nubian Christian kingdoms of Nobatia, Makuria, and Alodia (c. AD 543-1517) ruled the middle Nile for almost a millennium and formed one of the great African civilizations of the Middle Ages. After the collapse of Kush, three kingdoms emerged along the river: Nobatia in the north with its capital at Faras, Makuria centered on Dongola, and Alodia far to the south at Soba, near modern Khartoum. In the sixth century, missionaries sent with the support of the Byzantine empress Theodora and her rivals converted all three courts to Christianity.
para2: The kingdoms grew wealthy on the Nile trade and on diplomacy. Around 700 Makuria absorbed Nobatia, creating a powerful united kingdom that stretched from near Aswan deep into Sudan. Makuria's kings had already shown their strength in 651, when Nubian archers repelled the Arab army of Egypt at the Battle of Dongola; the peace treaty that followed, known as the Baqt, regulated relations between Christian Nubia and Muslim Egypt for some six centuries, one of the longest-lasting agreements in medieval history. Nubian churches and monasteries filled with painted decoration, and towns such as Faras and Old Dongola became centers of art, literacy, and royal ceremony.
para3: The kingdoms faced mounting pressure from the twelfth century onward. Saladin's brother led an Egyptian expedition into Nubia in the 1170s, Bedouin Arab tribes settled ever deeper in the riverlands, and the Mamluk sultans of Egypt intervened repeatedly in Makurian succession disputes, at one point capturing Dongola and installing a Muslim vassal king. Alodia held out longer in the south but gradually broke apart as well, its capital Soba falling around 1500 to Arab nomads and the rising Funj.
para4: By about 1517 the Christian Nubian kingdoms had vanished, replaced by Muslim sultanates, though Christian communities lingered for generations. Their rediscovery has been one of the triumphs of modern archaeology: Polish excavations at Faras uncovered a cathedral full of remarkable wall paintings now in Warsaw and Khartoum, and work at Old Dongola continues to reveal the splendor of a Christian African civilization that stood for a thousand years between medieval Egypt and the Sudanic world.
